subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: hiding the mistake and hoping it goes unnoticed [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday, evening.
The audit finished today. In March I typed the wrong tax rate into forty invoices. I didn't tell anyone. I opened each invoice and quietly changed it, no note, no reason. It took an evening, and I felt clever.
Today the auditors flagged edits with no explanation. Arnab, my manager, called me in. "Did you change these?" I said, "Yes, I fixed a typo." That wasn't the whole truth and Arnab knew it.
"The wrong rate," Arnab said, "I'd have fixed in a day. This I can't ignore." He didn't shout. That was worse.
I don't know if I'll get the same access again. I wish I'd walked to Arnab's desk in March.
— Hansa

qa.q: How many invoices did Hansa change quietly?
What was Hansa feeling while talking to Arnab?
qa.a: Hansa was ashamed and afraid, giving a half-truth and finding Arnab's quiet reaction worse than shouting.

qa.q: What could Hansa do now to begin rebuilding trust with Arnab?
qa.a: Hansa could give Arnab the full story, share a written account of every edit and offer to follow any check the team sets.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen the hidden edits compared with the original mistake?
qa.a: Arnab saw the original mistake as easy to fix in a day, but the silent edits as a breach of trust that could not be ignored.

grounding: The diary shows an employee who quietly patches an error and says nothing, so that when an audit finds it later the concealment harms trust more than the mistake.
